title: Sandtable Beacon
tagline: Throw a puck into the smoke: it ranges the phones of the people trapped inside, the building's twin turns rings into positions, and the tenant roster says who is still missing.
abstract: Beacon is the headline mode of Sandtable, the incident-command board for fire crews. A crew throws small UWB pucks (Qorvo DWM3001CDK boards) into a smoke-filled room. An occupant who opened the Beacon app on their iPhone is ranged by every puck over ultra-wideband, through Apple's Nearby Interaction accessory protocol, and the app sends a status with it: how many people, whether they can move, battery, floor. A locator fuses the ranges with the 3D twin's walls and is honest about geometry: one puck gives a ring, two give two candidates, the twin's walls or a third puck give a position. The building record's tenant roster is compared with the phones still inside, so the command agent gets an accountability table, search priorities and a report. Without the app a puck host can only count nearby Bluetooth devices, with no identities. Simulated end to end so far; the hardware path is written for tonight.
aha: A ring appears around the first puck: a trapped person's iPhone. The second puck, dropped carelessly, leaves two possible spots and the board says it cannot choose. Slide that puck to the wall and one spot falls outside the room: a position, and the tenant roster says how many people should still be in that suite.
how_it_works: An occupant opens the Beacon app on their iPhone and presses a status button (opt-in, random rotating id)
Each puck (Qorvo DWM3001CDK, stock firmware) ranges that iPhone over UWB through Apple's Nearby Interaction accessory protocol; the app posts each distance to the server
A locator fuses the ranges with the twin's walls: one puck a ring, two pucks two mirror spots, and the twin or the occupant's stated suite decides, visibly
The building record's tenant roster is joined to the twin's rooms and the phones: expected people, people reported inside, safe outside, unaccounted
A command agent turns that into radio orders, search priorities, where the next puck goes and record checks; an incident report closes the loop
Everything is published to the Sandtable command board as JSON, WebSocket, GeoJSON and Cursor-on-Target

Code-quality sweep with bug fixes. 334 tests pass. The host's baseline mode and the anchor flow have not run against the boards (the UNO Q was off). The demo left running on port 1885 was started on Saturday and runs that code until it is restarted.

left_hardware: 1. (5 min) hardware/BRINGUP.md step 1: power one DWM3001CDK and see whether it already ranges with Qorvo's free App Store app 'Qorvo Nearby Interaction'. If yes, skip flashing for that board.

2. (15 to 30 min incl. the email wait) BRINGUP step 0.1: download Qorvo's Nearby Interaction firmware (DWM3001CDK-QANI-FreeRTOS_full_QNI_3_0_0.hex, or the QANI hex in the DW3_QM33 SDK) from qorvo.com/products/d/da008212 or /da008582; use a work or school email. Keep the .hex in data/ or outside the repository.
3. (5 min first board, 2 min each after) hardware/FLASH.md: micro-USB DATA cable into port J9, SEGGER J-Flash Lite, device NRF52833_XXAA, erase, program, reset.
4. (5 min) BRINGUP step 3: prove one board and one iPhone with Qorvo's app; compare the distance with a tape measure.
5. (10 min) BRINGUP step 4: hotspot on the Android phone; laptop and both iPhones join it; `bash run_demo.sh --source live --lan` on the laptop.

6. (30 to 45 min) docs/IOS_BUILD.md and BRINGUP step 5: open apps/ios/SandtableBeacon.xcodeproj, choose your team, run on the iPhone 14; scan the board's QR code to fill in the server address; press Trapped: a ring appears on the board. If it does not compile, paste the errors back.

7. (20 min) BRINGUP step 6: puck A on a battery bank beside the UNO Q; puck B on the Android phone through USB-OTG into port J9; run the 10-minute soak test (does the phone or the bank cut the power?).
8. (10 min) BRINGUP step 7 and hardware/LAYOUT.md: tape the rectangle, stand both pucks just inside the door-wall edge, click them onto the plan, set the exercise scale: one position.
9. (10 min) BRINGUP step 8: second victim on the iPhone 15: 'Take turns' on both phones, or two more boards so each puck position has one board per phone.
10. (15 min) BRINGUP steps 9 and 10: rehearse the run-through twice and read the fallback ladder.

11. (30 min, optional, after step 7) hardware/BOARD_TO_BOARD.md: flash the TWR firmware on both boards (OpenOCD form that worked on the UNO Q), post the spacing with the host, anchor P1 and tap toward P2 on the board, then flash QANI back WITHOUT moving the boards. No TWR boards: tape-measure the spacing and post it with source manual

owner_questions.q: Can a UWB board range a victim's phone over UWB at all?
owner_questions.a: Yes, with exactly your boards: a Qorvo DWM3001CDK running Qorvo's stock Nearby Interaction firmware ranges an iPhone 11 or later through Apple's accessory protocol, once the person has opened our app. Both your iPhones give distance (about 60 readings a second); neither gives direction to an accessory. The app reads the distance and reports it; the board itself only logs it on its debug channel.

owner_questions.q: Can it be done cold, to a phone whose owner installed nothing?
owner_questions.a: No. An iPhone's UWB radio only answers a session started by an app with the user's permission. Cold, a radio can only count Bluetooth advertisements nearby: a rough band of devices by signal strength, no identity, and devices are not people. The stock puck firmware cannot even do that; the UNO Q's own radio can (written, never run).

owner_questions.q: One puck or two for angle?
owner_questions.a: Two pucks, as you chose, give one answer if you place them right. One puck gives a ring; two give two mirror spots across the line between the pucks, and an iPhone 14 or 15 reports no direction that could choose. Put both pucks just inside the wall the door is in (35 cm inside, about 4 m apart). Simulated over 800 phone positions in the room, with what a real iPhone delivers (distance only): one position in 76% of cases (35% because the twin rules the mirror spot out, 42% after the occupant's stated suite, shown as dismissed), median error 0.26 m, 1.5% of the positions shown wrong; the rest stay a ring (one puck did not reach the phone) or two spots. Pucks dropped mid-room: one position in only 4%, and the board says 'cannot choose' in 86%. Caveat: if the occupant states the wrong suite, the few positions that then appear are wrong. Better if you have it: a third puck gives one position in 84% with 0.20 m median error.

owner_questions.q: Will the phone keep answering with the screen off?
owner_questions.a: Not as built tonight: keep the app open (it keeps the screen awake). Two ways exist and are not built: a Bluetooth-paired background session in which only the puck gets the measurements, and, on iOS 18.4 or later, a Live Activity that lets the app keep ranging.

owner_questions.q: Can we put both UWB boards on one device we throw in?
owner_questions.a: It works poorly. The boards have one antenna each, so bearing can only come from the difference of two ranges. Simulated: at 10, 30 and 50 cm spacing the median bearing error is 37, 19 and 22 degrees (10 cm is no better than guessing), the sideways error 2.2, 1.5 and 1.4 m, the mirror ambiguity always remains, and the locator never publishes a position, only a ring. Two separate pucks 3 m apart: 7 degrees and 0.47 m sideways.

owner_questions.q: Two pucks: one on a battery bank with the UNO Q, one powered by the Android phone?
owner_questions.a: Yes, that is now the plan. Each board needs only 5 V. Puck A: battery bank, beside the UNO Q (which can run the server). Puck B: the Android phone over a USB-OTG adapter into the board's J-Link port (that port's chip shows up as a USB device, so the phone keeps the power on); keep a second bank as the fallback because some phones cut power to quiet devices. The phone cannot read the board (the stock firmware prints nothing on serial), and does not need to: the range returns through the iPhone app. The same phone can be the Wi-Fi hotspot for the laptop and both iPhones.

Power only (5 V on either micro-USB port). The range comes back through the iPhone app over Wi-Fi. Stand the board upright, at least 15 cm off the floor, component-free side toward the phone. Puck positions are measured with a tape and clicked onto the plan: the stock firmware cannot range board to board.

owner_questions.q: Two victims' iPhones on two pucks at once?
owner_questions.a: One iPhone can range both pucks at once. One board, on Qorvo's stock firmware, serves only one phone at a time (forum reports). So for two victims either the phones take turns (a switch in our app; simulated: a position after 3.5 s in the median, 9 s at the 90th percentile, and 23% of phones still without one after 24 s; untested on hardware), or each puck position carries two boards, one per phone (you have five boards; continuous ranging, no turn-taking). Prove one phone on both pucks first.

owner_questions.q: Where does the server run at the table, and how do the iPhones reach it?
owner_questions.a: On the laptop, with the laptop and both iPhones joined to a phone hotspot (venue Wi-Fi usually blocks device-to-device traffic); the Android phone powering puck B can be that hotspot. The board shows a QR code; scanning it with the iPhone camera opens our app with the server address filled in. Fallbacks: the server on the UNO Q on the same hotspot, or this machine over the tailnet if the iPhones run the tailnet client.

limitations: No phone has been ranged through our app yet: every phone result is simulated, with the noise model stated next to it. On the owner's UNO Q two boards have run Qorvo's phone firmware (advertising seen) and our board-to-board firmware (ranges measured).

An independent review found two faults that drew confident wrong positions (ranges kept after a puck moved; a two-puck position published without accounting for its mirror image). Both are fixed and a self-check now hunts for such cases; real hardware may reveal others.
The iOS app is uncompiled Swift source (written on a machine with no Mac); expect compiler errors on the first build.
Qorvo's firmware is not in this repository and cannot be: the owner downloads it from Qorvo.
Bring-up guides are written from documentation and forum reports, not from a board.
With Qorvo's stock firmware one board serves one phone at a time, and the range is read by the phone app, not by the puck: the phone needs a network path to the server and the app must stay open.
An iPhone 14 or 15 reports distance but no direction to an accessory.
A phone whose owner installed nothing cannot be ranged or identified; at most a rough count of Bluetooth devices nearby.

The building record is a public-data fixture (not CoStar data) and the twin is a synthetic interior (not a Matterport scan); expected head counts are estimates from floor area and building-code load factors.
The twin's rule-out of a spot 'two walls away' rests on an assumption of the range model (ranging through one wall at most) that the simulator shares; it has not been tested against real walls.
The command agent's plan in the walk-through is a recorded real model run; any other situation without a live model gets a deterministic fallback, labelled as such.

UNO Q: the simulated walk-through and the tests ran there (4 time-limit tests fail); live mode, the puck host and RTT reading have not run there. Its two boards last carried our board-to-board firmware, so an iPhone cannot range them until they are flashed with Qorvo's firmware again

Board to board: our TWR firmware and Qorvo's phone firmware cannot run on one board at once, so the spacing is measured at setup (or taped) and the boards must not move afterwards; the measured ranges are uncalibrated (unknown constant offset); running a TWR board next to a phone-ranging board (two boards per puck) is untested; one firmware doing both is not built; the host's baseline mode and the anchor flow have not run against the boards

Room and floor come from the responder's placement first; the phone's barometric pressure is carried but not turned into a floor; GPS is not used; UWB wall sensing is a research idea, not built (docs/ROOM_LOCATION.md)
